title: Vector analysis in special relativity
one_line_summary: Builds the four-vector toolkit of special relativity (component transformation law, index notation, basis vectors and their inverse transformation, Minkowski scalar product) and uses it to define four-velocity, four-momentum and four-acceleration, state four-momentum conservation, and treat photons, the Doppler shift and massless particles.
role_in_book: Chapter 1 gave the physics of special relativity through spacetime diagrams, the invariant interval and the Lorentz transformation. This chapter converts that physics into vector language and, above all, installs the index machinery (summation convention, dummy and free indices, barred indices for other frames, Lambda matrices, eta) that every later chapter relies on. It deliberately treats vectors provisionally (components that transform like coordinates) and flags eta as a future metric tensor, setting up Chapter 3's one-forms and tensors, Chapter 4's fluid four-vectors and conservation laws on hypersurfaces, and the curved-manifold redefinition of vectors in Chapters 5-6. The kinematic results (U.U = -1, U.a = 0, E = -p.U_obs, null photon momentum) are used without re-derivation throughout the GR chapters.

assumed_background.topic: Invariant interval and its classification into timelike, spacelike and null
Proper time along a timelike world line
Lorentz transformation for a boost along x
Spacetime diagrams of two observers, tilted axes, relativity of simultaneity
Geometrized units with c = 1 so velocities are dimensionless and energy, momentum and mass share units
Second postulate: light speed is the same in every inertial frame
Euclidean vectors as arrows with components, bases, linear combinations
Matrix multiplication, inverse matrices, identity matrix, linear independence
Derivatives along a curve and the product rule
Newtonian momentum, kinetic energy, conservation laws in collisions
Taylor expansion to low order (Newtonian limit of gamma)

learning_objectives: Reader can distinguish a four-vector (a frame-independent arrow) from its frame-dependent components and read the notation A ->_O (A^0, A^1, A^2, A^3).
Reader can apply the Einstein summation convention, identify free and dummy indices, rename them legally, and split a Greek sum into its time part plus a Latin spatial sum.
Reader can transform vector components between frames with A^alpha-bar = Lambda^alpha-bar_beta A^beta, writing down the 4x4 boost matrix for motion along x.
Reader can derive the basis-vector transformation law e_alpha = Lambda^beta-bar_alpha e_beta-bar from the frame independence of A^alpha e_alpha, and explain why it differs from the component law.

Reader can show that the inverse Lorentz transformation is the boost with reversed velocity, Lambda^nu_beta-bar(-v) Lambda^beta-bar_alpha(v) = delta^nu_alpha, and apply the rule that a Lambda's velocity is the motion of its upper-index frame as seen from its lower-index frame.
Reader can define four-velocity as the time basis vector of the (momentarily comoving) rest frame, compute its components gamma(1, v), and verify U.U = -1 and U = dx/dtau.
Reader can form four-momentum p = mU, identify p^0 as energy and recover rest energy plus Newtonian kinetic energy at low speed.
Reader can state four-momentum conservation and explain why frame-dependent 'before/after' bookkeeping for spacelike-separated collisions still gives one total vector.
Reader can compute Minkowski magnitudes and scalar products, classify vectors as timelike, spacelike or null, and prove invariance of the scalar product from invariance of magnitudes.
Reader can recognize Minkowski-orthogonal vectors on a spacetime diagram (mirror images about a light line) and explain why a null vector is orthogonal to itself.
Reader can show that four-acceleration is orthogonal to four-velocity and has only spatial components in the MCRF.
Reader can use p.p = -m^2 to get E^2 = m^2 + p^2 and compute the energy measured by any observer as -p.U_obs without changing frames.
Reader can explain why photons have no four-velocity or rest frame, build a null photon four-momentum, and derive the relativistic Doppler formula by boosting it.
Reader can argue that massive particles never reach light speed while massless particles always travel at it.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, notation-building chapter that alternates between index algebra and geometric pictures. Vectors are defined provisionally by how their components transform, yet the text insists at every step that the vector itself is a frame-free arrow and supplies diagrams (tilted bases, MCRF basis on a curved world line, orthogonal but non-perpendicular arrows) to keep that picture alive. Physical four-vectors are defined by what they look like in a privileged frame (rest frame, MCRF, observer's own frame) and then carried to other frames by Lorentz transformation or replaced by invariant dot products. Derivations are spelled out slowly with explicit coaching on dummy-index relabelling; the voice is conversational and first-person, and it repeatedly promises that the index positions and eta will be justified in later chapters.
narrative_arc: Provisional definition: a vector is anything whose components transform like coordinate differences; the displacement between two events is the prototype.
Notation toolkit: frame-labelled 'has components' arrow, bars on indices (not on the vector) for a new frame, Lambda matrix, Einstein summation, dummy versus free indices, Greek versus Latin ranges.
Vector algebra: component-wise addition and scaling, basis vectors of a frame, expansion A = A^alpha e_alpha.
Derive, rather than postulate, the basis transformation law from the frame independence of A, then check it on an explicit x-boost and draw both bases in one diagram (Figure 2.1).
Inverse transformations: argue physically that reversing the velocity undoes a boost, and show algebraically that the two Lambda matrices multiply to the Kronecker delta.

Physical vectors: four-velocity as e_0 of the rest frame, extended to accelerated motion with the MCRF (Figure 2.2); four-momentum p = mU with a low-speed check that justifies the names velocity, momentum, energy.
Postulate conservation of total four-momentum, then confront the simultaneity puzzle for spacelike-separated collisions (Figure 2.3) and resolve it; define the CM frame.

Geometry: magnitude by analogy with the interval, scalar product and its invariance via the polarization identity, timelike/spacelike/null classes, orthogonality that is not perpendicularity (Figure 2.4), eta as a generalized Kronecker delta.
Applications: U = dx/dtau (Figure 2.5), four-acceleration orthogonal to U, E^2 = m^2 + p^2, and observer-measured energy as the invariant -p.U_obs.
Photons: null world lines forbid a four-velocity, null four-momentum with |p| = E, Doppler shift from a boost plus E = h nu, massless particles and the unreachable light speed for massive ones.

Exercises extend to boost composition and non-symmetric products, uniform acceleration and relativistic rockets, particle reactions, Compton and inverse-Compton scattering, and orthonormality of boosted bases.
signature_moves: Separating object from representation typographically: an arrow over the symbol for the vector, a labelled arrow 'has components in frame O' for its components, and bars on indices so the vector symbol never changes between frames.
Defining a physical four-vector by its trivially simple form in a special frame (U = e_0 of the rest frame or MCRF; p^0 = E in the observer's frame) and letting the transformation law do the rest.
Extracting a law from an identity valid for an arbitrary vector: relabel dummy indices until the arbitrary components factor out, then set each coefficient to zero.
Proving invariance by bootstrapping from a known invariant (magnitudes are invariant, so the cross term in (A+B)^2 must be too) instead of grinding matrix algebra.
Naming justified by the Newtonian limit: spatial components of U and p reduce to v and mv, and p^0 to m plus kinetic energy.
Explicit bookkeeping rule for Lambda: its velocity argument is how fast the frame named by the upper index moves as seen from the frame named by the lower index.
Steering the reader toward invariant scalar expressions (-p.U_obs) and later testing the payoff in an exercise that compares with brute-force transformation.
Anticipatory honesty: tells the reader that index positions, eta, and the definition of a vector will all be revisited more satisfactorily later.

sections.title: Definition of a vector
sections.summary: Adopts the Euclidean-style working definition of a vector as a set of components that change under a frame change exactly as coordinate differences do. The displacement between two events is the model case. The section introduces the notation that separates a vector from its components, writes the Lorentz transformation as a linear sum with coefficients Lambda, and uses it to motivate the summation convention, dummy and free indices, and the Greek/Latin index ranges. A general vector is then any four same-dimensioned numbers in one frame plus this transformation rule; addition and scalar multiplication work component-wise. Footnotes (recovered from the page renders) call the frame change a passive transformation and introduce the terms four-vector and three-vector.
key_moves: Write the displacement's components in O and in O-bar, putting the bar on the index because the vector itself is unchanged.
Rewrite the boost formula for the time component as a sum of four coefficients times components, and generalize to all components (Eq. 2.3).
Drop the sigma using the summation convention (Eq. 2.4), with examples of what does and does not sum.
Show dummy indices may be renamed but not to a Latin index, giving the split in Eq. 2.5.
Show a free index represents four equations and must be renamed consistently on both sides.
Define a general vector by components in one frame plus the rule A^alpha-bar = Lambda^alpha-bar_beta A^beta (Eqs. 2.6-2.7); note all components must share dimensions.

sections.title: Vector algebra
sections.summary: Defines the four basis vectors of a frame by their components, expresses any vector as a linear combination of them, and derives how the basis vectors of one frame are written in terms of another's. A worked x-boost computes both new components of a sample vector and the old basis in terms of the new, and Figure 2.1 draws both bases from the moving observer's viewpoint. The section notes that pure-boost matrices are symmetric, then treats inverse transformations: reversing the velocity undoes a boost, and the product of the two matrices is the Kronecker delta, which also inverts the component law.
concepts: basis vectors of an inertial frame
key_moves: Define e_alpha by (e_alpha)^beta = delta_alpha^beta and show A = A^alpha e_alpha (Eqs. 2.9-2.11).
Insist the same vector equals A^alpha-bar e_alpha-bar in O-bar, stressing that barred and unbarred indices are not interchangeable (Eq. 2.12).
Substitute the component law, reorder the finite sums, relabel dummy indices to factor out arbitrary A^alpha, and conclude e_alpha = Lambda^beta-bar_alpha e_beta-bar (Eq. 2.13).
Worked boost: components of (5,0,0,2) become (5 gamma, -5v gamma, 0, 2); e_0 = gamma e_0-bar - v gamma e_1-bar, e_1 = -v gamma e_0-bar + gamma e_1-bar.
Draw both bases in O-bar's diagram (Figure 2.1) and note the boost matrix is symmetric, a property of all pure boosts.

Make the velocity dependence explicit, argue the reverse transformation uses -v (Eqs. 2.14-2.15), substitute to get an identity in O's basis alone (Eq. 2.16), and read off Lambda(-v) Lambda(v) = delta (Eq. 2.18).
Apply the inverse to components, recovering A^nu from A^beta-bar.

sections.title: The four-velocity
sections.summary: Generalizes the Galilean velocity (tangent to a path) to the four-velocity: a tangent to the world line whose length is one unit of the particle's own time, which makes it the time basis vector of the particle's inertial rest frame. For accelerated particles the momentarily comoving reference frame (MCRF) supplies the rest frame at each event; MCRFs at an event are unique up to spatial rotation. Figure 2.2 shows the MCRF basis at one event of a curved world line.
key_moves: Define U as a unit-time-length tangent to the world line.
Observe that in the rest frame this is exactly e_0, giving an equivalent definition.
Introduce the MCRF for accelerated motion and note the rotational ambiguity is harmless.
Define U of an accelerated particle as e_0 of its MCRF at that event (Figure 2.2).

sections.title: The four-momentum and its conservation
sections.summary: Defines four-momentum as rest mass times four-velocity, names its time component the energy and its spatial components the momentum, and checks the names by boosting from the rest frame and expanding at low speed. Conservation of the total four-momentum of interacting particles is postulated as the natural relativistic generalization of Newtonian energy and momentum conservation, with the striking prediction that rest mass can be converted to heat. The text then worries about what 'at a given time' means when collisions are spacelike separated (Figure 2.3) and shows every observer's slice yields the same total vector. The centre-of-momentum frame is defined.
key_moves: Define p = mU with components (E, p^1, p^2, p^3) (Eqs. 2.19-2.20).
Example: U^alpha = Lambda^alpha_0-bar from the rest frame gives U = gamma(1, v, 0, 0) and p = m gamma(1, v, 0, 0) (Eq. 2.21).
Expand E = m gamma at small v to get m + mv^2/2.
Postulate conservation of summed four-momentum (Eq. 2.22) as an extra, experimentally supported law.
Use Figure 2.3 to show observers tally different sets of particles on their constant-time slices, but local conservation at each collision makes the total vector identical.
Define the CM frame as the frame where the total spatial momentum vanishes (Eq. 2.23).

sections.title: Scalar product
sections.summary: Defines the magnitude of a vector by the interval formula, guaranteed invariant because components transform like coordinate differences, and classifies vectors as spacelike, null or timelike, warning that a null vector is not the zero vector. The scalar product is defined in one frame and proven frame independent from invariance of magnitudes. Orthogonality is defined by a vanishing dot product; examples show the basis of any frame is an orthonormal tetrad summarized by eta, that a moving frame's basis vectors are orthogonal though not perpendicular on the diagram (Figure 2.4), and that U.U = -1.
concepts: Lorentz invariance of the scalar product
key_moves: Define A^2 with a minus sign on the time component and note invariance is automatic (Eqs. 2.24-2.25).
Classify by sign; stress null is not zero because the form is indefinite.
Define A.B (Eq. 2.26) and prove invariance via (A+B)^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2A.B.
Note orthogonal vectors need not look perpendicular and null vectors are self-orthogonal.
Compute e_alpha.e_beta = eta_alpha-beta (Eq. 2.27) and flag eta as the future metric tensor.
Apply to O-bar's basis in O's diagram with the equal-angles-to-the-light-line rule (Figure 2.4).
Conclude U.U = -1 since U is some frame's e_0 (Eq. 2.28).

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Uses the scalar product to recast earlier results. The interval is the magnitude of the infinitesimal displacement and proper time is its negative; dx/dtau is a unit timelike tangent equal to e_0 of the MCRF, so U = dx/dtau (Figure 2.5). Differentiating U.U = -1 shows the four-acceleration dU/dtau is orthogonal to U and purely spatial in the MCRF. For momentum, p.p = -m^2 gives E^2 = m^2 + p^2, and the energy any observer measures is -p.U_obs, a frame-independent recipe.
key_moves: Identify ds^2 = dx.dx and dtau^2 = -dx.dx (Eqs. 2.29-2.30).
Show dx/dtau has magnitude -1 and equals (1,0,0,0) in the MCRF, hence U = dx/dtau (Eq. 2.31).
Differentiate U.U = -1 to get U.dU/dtau = 0 and define a with U.a = 0 (Eq. 2.32).
Compute p.p = -m^2 and expand to E^2 = m^2 + sum (p^i)^2 (Eqs. 2.33-2.34).
Evaluate p.U_obs in the observer's frame where U_obs = e_0-bar to get E-bar = -p.U_obs (Eq. 2.35).

sections.title: Photons
sections.summary: Photons travel on null lines, so proper time vanishes, no unit tangent exists, and there is no MCRF: the four-velocity is undefined, though tangent vectors like dx still exist. A photon's four-momentum is fixed by its energy and nullness, so its spatial momentum equals its energy. With E = h nu, a single boost gives the relativistic Doppler formula. Null four-momentum is equivalent to zero rest mass; the photon is the only known massless particle (neutrinos are light but massive, and the graviton is not yet a well-defined notion). Massive particles have p/E below one at any energy and so always possess a rest frame.
concepts: light speed as an unreachable limit for massive particles
key_moves: From dx.dx = 0 infer dtau = 0, so Eq. 2.31 fails; restate via the second postulate (no frame where light is at rest) (Eq. 2.36).
Set p^0 = E and demand a null vector along x to get p^x = E (Eq. 2.37).
Boost p along x and use E = h nu in both frames to get nu-bar/nu = sqrt((1-v)/(1+v)) (Eqs. 2.38-2.39).
Show m^2 = -p.p = 0 for photons and that null momentum and zero mass imply each other (Eq. 2.40).
For m not zero, p^1/p^0 = sqrt(1 - m^2/(p^0)^2) < 1, so the frame moving at p^1/p^0 is a rest frame.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: A two-sentence pointer noting that relativistic kinematics and particle dynamics have only been sampled, that particle physics furnishes the sharpest tests of special relativity, and recommending Hagedorn (1963) and Wiedemann (2007).
key_moves: Points to particle-physics kinematics texts for further study.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Thirty-five exercises (2.1-2.35, ending on printed p.55). Early ones drill index manipulation and component transformations; middle ones address inverse and composed boosts, four-velocity from three-velocity, velocity addition, classification and orthogonality proofs; later ones cover uniform acceleration and a relativistic rocket trip, particle reactions and CM frames, Doppler shifts at an angle, energy needed to approach light speed, heat adding inertia, invariant energy measurement, radiation pressure on a mirror, Compton scattering and inverse-Compton upscattering of the microwave background, and orthonormality of a boosted basis.
key_moves: Practice summation and index renaming with explicit number arrays.
Compose two non-collinear boosts and interpret the non-symmetric product.
Model a constantly accelerating rocket and compute proper time to the Galactic centre.
Apply four-momentum conservation to forbid single-photon pair annihilation and to derive the Compton formula.
Compare brute-force frame transformation with the invariant -p.U_obs shortcut.

concepts.name: four-vector
concepts.definition: An object in Minkowski spacetime given by four components in one inertial frame, whose components in any other inertial frame are obtained by applying the same Lorentz transformation that acts on coordinate differences; the four components must share one physical dimension because a boost mixes them.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a provisional definition borrowed from Euclidean geometry, with the displacement between events as the prototype; after the index notation is built, any four numbers in one frame plus the rule A^alpha-bar = Lambda^alpha-bar_beta A^beta define a vector. The author promises a better definition later.
concepts.notes: Footnote 2 (on printed p.35, dropped by the export) introduces the words four-vector and three-vector and the convention of arrows for four-vectors and boldface for three-vectors.

concepts.name: displacement vector
concepts.definition: The four-vector running from one event to another; its components in a frame are the coordinate differences (Delta t, Delta x, Delta y, Delta z), and its infinitesimal version dx is tangent to a world line.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the chapter as the typical vector whose transformation law is literally the Lorentz transformation of coordinate differences; reappears in §2.6 as the infinitesimal step dx whose magnitude is the interval.
formulas: \Delta\vec x \underset{\mathcal O}{\to} (\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)

concepts.name: vector as a geometric object
concepts.definition: A vector is a single frame-independent entity (picturable as an arrow between events); its components are coordinate-dependent numbers obtained by referring it to a particular frame's basis, so a frame change alters components but never the vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Enforced through notation: an arrow marks the vector, a labelled arrow means 'has components in frame O', and bars go on indices instead of the vector symbol. Reinforced by A^alpha e_alpha = A^alpha-bar e_alpha-bar: different pieces, same sum.

concepts.name: passive transformation
concepts.definition: A change of description in which the coordinates, and hence the components, change while the vector itself stays fixed, as opposed to an active transformation that moves or rotates the vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Footnote 1 on printed p.34 (missing from the export, recovered from the render) ties the frame change of components to this linear-algebra term.

concepts.name: Lorentz transformation matrix
concepts.definition: The 4x4 array Lambda^alpha-bar_beta of numbers that converts a vector's components in frame O into its components in frame O-bar; for a boost of speed v along x its t-x block has gamma on the diagonal and -v gamma off the diagonal, with 1 for the y and z entries.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off by writing Chapter 1's boost formula for Delta t-bar as a linear sum with four coefficients, then generalizing to all components (16 numbers); written out as a matrix in the first worked example.
concepts.notes: Why one index is up and one down is explicitly deferred to the differential-geometry chapters.

concepts.name: Einstein summation convention
concepts.definition: When an index letter appears once as a superscript and once as a subscript in the same term, a sum over all values of that index is understood; repeated indices at the same level, or different letters, imply no sum.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to abbreviate the Lorentz transformation sum, illustrated with pairs of expressions that do and do not sum.

concepts.name: dummy index
concepts.definition: An index that is summed over within a term; its letter carries no meaning and may be changed to any other letter with the same range without altering the expression.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by rewriting Eq. 2.4 with a different summed letter, with the single restriction that a Greek dummy cannot become Latin; later the relabelling of dummies is singled out as the decisive trick in deriving the basis transformation law.

concepts.name: free index
concepts.definition: An index that is not summed; an equation carrying free indices stands for one equation per value of each, and a free index must bear the same name in every term, being renamed everywhere at once if at all.
concepts.how_introduced: Eq. 2.4 is read as four equations; a consistent renaming is contrasted with an illegal one that renames only the left-hand side.

concepts.name: Greek and Latin index ranges
concepts.definition: Greek indices take the values 0, 1, 2, 3 and Latin indices only 1, 2, 3, so a sum on a Greek index equals its 0 term plus the corresponding Latin (spatial) sum.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the one forbidden dummy relabelling and captured in Eq. 2.5.

concepts.name: vector space operations on four-vectors
concepts.definition: Four-vectors add component by component and scale by real numbers, the results again being four-vectors; the set of four-vectors is therefore a four-dimensional real vector space.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated via components in one frame (Eq. 2.8), noting that because the transformation is linear these operations commute with frame changes.
formulas: \vec A+\vec B\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(A^0+B^0,\dots,A^3+B^3),\quad \mu\vec A\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(\mu A^0,\dots,\mu A^3)

concepts.name: basis vectors of an inertial frame
concepts.definition: The four vectors e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3 of an inertial frame whose components in that same frame are the columns of the identity matrix; each points along one coordinate axis, and every vector is the combination A^alpha e_alpha of them with its components as coefficients.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by their components in their own frame; the text notes e_0-bar differs from e_0 because they belong to different frames and that the basis index must be written low to use the summation convention.

concepts.name: Kronecker delta
concepts.definition: The symbol delta^beta_alpha equal to 1 when its indices coincide and 0 otherwise; as a matrix it is the identity, and summing it against a vector index just renames that index.
concepts.how_introduced: Packages the components of the basis vectors (Eq. 2.10) and reappears as the identity matrix that certifies Lambda(-v) as the inverse of Lambda(v).

concepts.name: transformation law for basis vectors
concepts.definition: The basis of frame O is expressed through that of O-bar as e_alpha = Lambda^beta-bar_alpha e_beta-bar, summing over the matrix's upper index; this is the inverse pattern to the component law, which is exactly what keeps A^alpha e_alpha unchanged.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by demanding that A^alpha e_alpha equal A^alpha-bar e_alpha-bar for every vector, substituting the component law, relabelling dummy indices so the arbitrary components factor out, and setting each bracket to zero; checked on an x-boost and drawn in Figure 2.1.
prerequisites: basis vectors of an inertial frame

concepts.name: inverse Lorentz transformation
concepts.definition: The matrix taking components from O-bar back to O is the same boost with the velocity reversed, and the two matrices multiply to the identity: Lambda^nu_beta-bar(-v) Lambda^beta-bar_alpha(v) = delta^nu_alpha.
concepts.how_introduced: Physical argument first (O moves at -v relative to O-bar, Eq. 2.15); then substitution into Eq. 2.14 produces a relation among O's basis vectors alone that is only consistent if the matrix product is the Kronecker delta; finally applied to components.
concepts.notes: Bookkeeping rule given in the text: a Lambda's velocity argument describes how the frame carrying its upper index moves when viewed from the frame carrying its lower index.

concepts.name: matrix multiplication as index contraction
concepts.definition: A sum over an index shared by two arrays, such as Lambda^nu_beta-bar Lambda^beta-bar_alpha, is precisely the row-times-column rule of matrix multiplication, so index expressions can be checked as matrix products.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out when Eq. 2.18 is identified as a statement that two matrices are inverse; used again in Exercise 2.13 for composed boosts.

concepts.name: symmetry of pure boost matrices
concepts.definition: The Lorentz matrix of a pure boost, in any direction and with no relative rotation of spatial axes, equals its own transpose; a Lorentz matrix that is not symmetric therefore includes a rotation.
concepts.how_introduced: Noticed in the x-boost example and asserted for general directions; Exercise 2.13 has the reader compose two perpendicular boosts, find a non-symmetric and order-dependent product, and interpret it.
concepts.notes: The book does not name the resulting rotation (Thomas-Wigner rotation).

concepts.name: four-velocity
concepts.definition: The unit timelike vector tangent to a particle's world line, equal to the time basis vector of its rest frame or MCRF and to dx/dtau; for three-velocity v its components are gamma(1, v) and it always satisfies U.U = -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalizes the Galilean velocity as a path tangent: tangent to the world line and one unit of the particle's own time long, hence e_0 of its rest frame; accelerated particles use the MCRF; §2.6 shows it equals dx/dtau.
prerequisites: basis vectors of an inertial frame

concepts.name: three-velocity
concepts.definition: A particle's ordinary velocity dx/dt measured in a chosen frame; the spatial components of the four-velocity equal gamma times it, so they approach it at low speed.
concepts.how_introduced: Named to contrast with four-velocity; the link is shown in the worked example leading to Eq. 2.21 and in Exercise 2.15.

concepts.name: momentarily comoving reference frame
concepts.definition: For a particle at a given event, an inertial frame moving with the particle's instantaneous velocity so that the particle is momentarily at rest in it; it ceases to be comoving an instant later if the particle accelerates, and is unique only up to spatial rotations.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed because an accelerated particle has no single inertial rest frame; Figure 2.2 draws the MCRF basis at one event on a curved world line, with its time basis vector tangent to the curve.
concepts.notes: Becomes the workhorse for fluid elements in Chapter 4.

concepts.name: rest mass
concepts.definition: The mass of a particle measured in its own rest frame; a Lorentz scalar that equals the square root of -p.p and vanishes for photons.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in passing in the definition p = mU; recovered invariantly from p.p = -m^2 in §2.6 and shown to be zero for null momenta in §2.7.

concepts.name: four-momentum
concepts.definition: The four-vector p = mU of a massive particle (a null vector for a photon) whose time component in a frame is the particle's energy there and whose spatial components are its momentum there.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as rest mass times four-velocity; components for motion along x obtained by transforming from the rest frame (Eq. 2.21), with names justified by the low-speed limit.

concepts.name: relativistic energy
concepts.definition: The time component E = p^0 = gamma m of four-momentum in a given frame; it includes the rest-mass energy m and approaches m + mv^2/2 at low speed.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the zeroth component and justified by a binomial expansion showing rest energy plus the Galilean kinetic energy.

concepts.name: conservation of four-momentum
concepts.definition: In any interaction the vector sum of the four-momenta of all particles is the same before and after; equivalently energy (including rest mass) and every momentum component are conserved in every inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Postulated because its components reduce to the Newtonian conservation laws; described as an extra postulate among many possible generalizations, selected by experiment. The 'before/after' ambiguity for spacelike-separated collisions is raised and resolved using Figure 2.3.

concepts.name: mass–energy conversion
concepts.definition: Because conserved energy includes rest mass, the total rest mass of a system can decrease in a reaction with the difference emerging as kinetic energy or heat; conversely adding heat to a body raises its rest mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as one of the notable new predictions of four-momentum conservation with nuclear power as the everyday case; Exercise 2.27 runs it in reverse with a heated body.

concepts.name: relativity of simultaneity
concepts.definition: Events simultaneous in one inertial frame need not be simultaneous in another, and spacelike-separated events can occur in either order depending on the frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 1 to pose the puzzle of which particles to include when totalling momentum 'at one time' (Figure 2.3).

concepts.name: hypersurface of constant time
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional set of events that a given inertial observer regards as simultaneous (t = const); different observers' slices are tilted with respect to each other in spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced while explaining that any observer may choose a slice, total the momenta crossing it, and obtain the same vector because each collision conserves momentum locally; flagged as a structure that returns with later conservation laws.

concepts.name: centre of momentum frame
concepts.definition: An inertial frame in which the total spatial momentum of a system is zero, so the total four-momentum has only a time component equal to the total energy; any frame at rest relative to it also qualifies.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by its component form right after the conservation discussion, with the remark that like MCRFs it is fixed only up to spatial orientation.

concepts.name: magnitude of a four-vector
concepts.definition: The Lorentz-invariant number obtained by subtracting the squared time component from the sum of the three squared spatial components (A.A with the Minkowski signs); it may be positive, zero or negative, and Schutz calls this signed quantity itself the magnitude rather than taking a square root.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by analogy with the interval; invariance needs no proof because components were defined to transform like coordinate differences.

concepts.name: timelike, spacelike and null vectors
concepts.definition: A vector is spacelike if its magnitude is positive, null if its magnitude is zero while its components are not all zero, and timelike if its magnitude is negative; the label is the same in every frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over directly from the names for intervals in Chapter 1.

concepts.name: null vector versus zero vector
concepts.definition: A null vector has zero magnitude but non-vanishing components (it points along the light cone) and is orthogonal to itself; the zero vector has every component zero. Only for a positive-definite inner product does zero magnitude force the zero vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Emphasized immediately after the classification and again in the discussion of orthogonality and photon momenta.

concepts.name: scalar product of four-vectors
concepts.definition: The frame-independent, bilinear and symmetric number formed from two vectors by multiplying matching components, giving the time-time product a minus sign and the three space-space products plus signs; with both vectors equal it reduces to the magnitude.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in one frame and then proved invariant using only the invariance of magnitudes; its linearity properties are left to Exercise 2.34.

concepts.name: Lorentz invariance of the scalar product
concepts.definition: The scalar product takes the same value whichever inertial frame's components are used, because (A+B)^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2A.B and each magnitude is already invariant.
concepts.how_introduced: A three-line proof built entirely on invariance of magnitudes, avoiding explicit matrix computation.
formulas: (\vec A+\vec B)^2=\vec A^2+\vec B^2+2\vec A\cdot\vec B

concepts.name: orthogonality in Minkowski spacetime
concepts.definition: Two vectors are orthogonal when their scalar product vanishes. In a t-x spacetime diagram such a pair appears as mirror images across a 45-degree light line rather than at a right angle, and a null vector is orthogonal to itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined algebraically, then visualized with the basis vectors of a moving frame drawn in the rest frame's diagram (Figure 2.4) and summarized by the equal-angles-with-the-light-ray rule.

concepts.name: orthonormal tetrad
concepts.definition: Four mutually orthogonal vectors, one timelike of magnitude -1 and three spacelike of magnitude +1; the basis of every inertial frame is such a tetrad.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by computing the dot products of a frame's basis vectors; Exercise 2.35 asks the reader to confirm that a boosted basis still satisfies the same relations.
prerequisites: basis vectors of an inertial frame
concepts.notes: A timelike vector counts as unit when its magnitude is -1.

concepts.name: Minkowski metric components
concepts.definition: The numbers eta_alpha-beta = e_alpha.e_beta, forming diag(-1, 1, 1, 1) in any inertial basis, so that A.B = eta_alpha-beta A^alpha B^beta.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a Kronecker-delta-like symbol with -1 in the time slot, explicitly flagged as the metric tensor to be developed later.

concepts.name: normalization of four-velocity
concepts.definition: Every four-velocity has scalar product -1 with itself, because it is the time basis vector of some inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as an example of orthonormality (Eq. 2.28) and re-derived from dx/dtau in §2.6; differentiating it yields the orthogonality of four-acceleration.

concepts.name: invariant interval
concepts.definition: The frame-independent separation ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 between nearby events, now recognized as the magnitude of the displacement vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 1 (Eq. 1.1) and rewritten as dx.dx.

concepts.name: proper time
concepts.definition: The time recorded by a clock moving along a timelike world line, given for an infinitesimal step by dtau^2 = -dx.dx.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 1 (Eq. 1.9), restated with the scalar product, and used to parametrize world lines so that dx/dtau is unit.

concepts.name: four-acceleration
concepts.definition: The derivative a = dU/dtau of four-velocity with respect to proper time; it is always orthogonal to U, so in the MCRF it has zero time component and spatial components equal to the acceleration the particle itself measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Differentiating U.U = -1 gives U.dU/dtau = 0; since U is purely temporal in the MCRF, the derivative must be purely spatial there. The name is justified in Exercise 2.19.

concepts.name: energy–momentum relation
concepts.definition: For any particle E^2 = m^2 + |p|^2 in units with c = 1; it is the component form of p.p = -m^2 and holds with m = 0 for photons.
concepts.how_introduced: Two lines: scale U.U = -1 by m^2, then expand the dot product in components.

concepts.name: energy measured by an observer
concepts.definition: An observer with four-velocity U_obs assigns a particle of four-momentum p the energy E-bar = -p.U_obs; being a scalar, it can be evaluated with components in any frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Since U_obs is the observer's own time basis vector, the dot product picks out the time component of p in the observer's frame; the text advises using such invariant forms in calculations, and Exercise 2.30 compares this route with explicit transformation.

concepts.name: absence of photon four-velocity
concepts.definition: A photon has no four-velocity: its world line is null, so dtau = 0 and no tangent of unit magnitude exists, and by the second postulate there is no inertial frame in which light is at rest. Tangent vectors of zero magnitude, such as dx, still exist.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued twice, from the failure of U = dx/dtau and from the second postulate, with a careful note that the problem is normalization, not tangency.

concepts.name: photon four-momentum
concepts.definition: A photon's four-momentum is a null vector parallel to its world line; its time component is the energy E and its spatial momentum has magnitude E, so for motion along x it is (E, E, 0, 0).
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed by combining p^0 = E with the requirement of being parallel to a null world line, hence null.

concepts.name: Planck relation
concepts.definition: A photon's energy equals Planck's constant times its frequency.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from quantum mechanics as the bridge from four-momentum to frequency.
concepts.notes: The printed unit for h is J s^-1; it should be J s.

concepts.name: relativistic Doppler shift
concepts.definition: Light's frequency depends on the frame: an observer moving at speed v along a photon's direction of travel measures nu-bar/nu = sqrt((1-v)/(1+v)); for a photon at angle theta to the boost direction nu-bar/nu = (1 - v cos theta)/sqrt(1-v^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Two lines: Lorentz-transform the photon's four-momentum and apply E = h nu in each frame; generalized to arbitrary angle in Exercise 2.25, which also asks for a derivation from -p.U_obs.

concepts.name: transverse Doppler shift
concepts.definition: The frequency change that survives when the photon moves perpendicular to the relative velocity as described in the original frame, a pure time-dilation effect.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 2.25(b), which also asks at what angle the shift vanishes.

concepts.name: zero rest-mass particles
concepts.definition: Particles whose four-momentum is null, equivalently whose rest mass is zero; they always move at light speed and have no rest frame. The photon is the only confirmed example; neutrinos are very light but massive.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced from m^2 = -p.p = 0 for photons and stated as a two-way equivalence.

concepts.name: light speed as an unreachable limit for massive particles
concepts.definition: For m not zero, p^1/p^0 = sqrt(1 - m^2/E^2) is below 1 at every finite energy, so a massive particle never attains light speed and always has a rest frame moving at velocity p/E.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from p.p = -m^2 alongside the observation that the energy would have to diverge; Exercise 2.26 quantifies the diverging energy cost.

concepts.name: graviton
concepts.definition: The hypothetical massless quantum associated with gravitational waves; the text cautions it is not yet well defined because no satisfactory quantum theory of gravity exists.
concepts.how_introduced: A parenthetical aside in the list of massless particles, noting that gravitational waves also move at light speed.

concepts.name: composition of Lorentz boosts
concepts.definition: The transformation between frames related by two successive boosts is the matrix product of the individual Lorentz matrices; for non-collinear boosts the product is non-symmetric and order-dependent, meaning it contains a spatial rotation in addition to a boost.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 2.13 with speeds 0.6 along x then 0.8 along the intermediate frame's y axis, asking for invariance checks and interpretation of the asymmetry and non-commutativity.

concepts.name: uniform acceleration
concepts.definition: Motion whose four-acceleration has constant magnitude and fixed spatial direction, so the acceleration felt in each MCRF never changes; the world line is a hyperbola such as t = a sinh(tau/a), x = a cosh(tau/a) with proper acceleration 1/a.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 2.19 (a rocket at about one Earth gravity, including a trip to the Galactic centre) and 2.21 (the hyperbolic world line parametrized by proper time).

concepts.name: Compton scattering
concepts.definition: Scattering of a photon from a charged particle initially at rest, after which the photon's frequency obeys 1/nu_f = 1/nu_i + h(1 - cos theta)/m (c = 1), a direct consequence of four-momentum conservation.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 2.32 derives the formula; Exercise 2.33 applies it in the rest frame of an ultra-energetic cosmic-ray proton scattering a microwave-background photon.

concepts.name: velocity addition from four-velocity
concepts.definition: Boosting a particle's four-velocity and taking the ratio of spatial to time components in the new frame reproduces the relativistic velocity-addition law.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 2.16, revisiting Chapter 1's result with the new machinery.

concepts.name: linear independence
concepts.definition: A set of vectors is linearly independent if the only linear combination of them giving the zero vector has all coefficients zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Exercise 2.5, which asks for a proof that a frame's basis is independent.

key_equations.name: Displacement components
key_equations.latex: \Delta\vec x\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)
key_equations.meaning: The separation vector between two events has the coordinate differences as its components in frame O.
key_equations.symbols: labelled arrow = has components in frame O

key_equations.name: Compact component notation
key_equations.latex: \Delta\vec x\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}\{\Delta x^{\alpha}\},\qquad \Delta\vec x\underset{\bar{\mathcal O}}{\to}\{\Delta x^{\bar\alpha}\}
key_equations.meaning: Braces denote the full set of four components; a bar on the index, not on the vector, signals components in another frame.

key_equations.name: Boost of the time component
key_equations.meaning: Chapter 1's Lorentz transformation written as a linear combination, revealing the coefficients Lambda^0-bar_beta = (gamma, -v gamma, 0, 0).

key_equations.name: Lorentz transformation with explicit sum
key_equations.meaning: Every new component is a fixed linear combination of the old ones; the 16 coefficients form the Lorentz matrix.

key_equations.name: Lorentz transformation (summation convention)
key_equations.meaning: Same statement with the sum implied by the repeated upper/lower index beta; alpha-bar is free, so this is four equations.

key_equations.name: Greek sum split into time and space
key_equations.meaning: A sum on a Greek index equals the 0 term plus a sum on a Latin index running 1..3, which is why a Greek dummy may not be renamed Latin.

key_equations.name: Vector given by components
key_equations.meaning: A general vector is specified by four numbers in one frame.

key_equations.name: Component transformation law
key_equations.meaning: Defining property of a four-vector: its components change exactly as coordinate differences do.

key_equations.name: Vector addition and scaling
key_equations.latex: \vec A+\vec B\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(A^0+B^0,\,A^1+B^1,\,A^2+B^2,\,A^3+B^3),\qquad \mu\vec A\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(\mu A^0,\mu A^1,\mu A^2,\mu A^3)
key_equations.meaning: Four-vectors form a vector space with component-wise operations.

key_equations.name: Basis vectors of O
key_equations.latex: \vec e_0\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(1,0,0,0),\ \vec e_1\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(0,1,0,0),\ \vec e_2\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(0,0,1,0),\ \vec e_3\underset{\mathcal O}{\to}(0,0,0,1)
key_equations.meaning: Each basis vector of a frame has a single unit component in that frame.

key_equations.name: Basis components as Kronecker delta
key_equations.meaning: Compact form of Eq. 2.9.

key_equations.name: Expansion in a basis
key_equations.latex: \vec A=A^{0}\vec e_0+A^1\vec e_1+A^2\vec e_2+A^3\vec e_3=A^{\alpha}\vec e_{\alpha}
key_equations.meaning: Components are the coefficients of the vector along the frame's basis vectors.

key_equations.name: Frame independence of the expansion
key_equations.meaning: Different component sets and different bases combine to the same vector; barred and unbarred indices are not interchangeable.

key_equations.name: Intermediate step with factored components
key_equations.meaning: After relabelling dummies, the arbitrary components multiply a bracket that must therefore vanish for each alpha.

key_equations.name: Basis transformation law
key_equations.meaning: Old basis vectors as combinations of new ones; note the sum is on the upper index of Lambda, unlike the component law.

key_equations.name: Boost matrix along x
key_equations.meaning: Explicit Lorentz matrix for O-bar moving at v along x relative to O; symmetric, as for every pure boost.

key_equations.name: Boosted components of the sample vector
key_equations.meaning: Worked numerical application of Eq. 2.7.

key_equations.name: O's basis in terms of O-bar's
key_equations.latex: \vec e_0=\gamma\vec e_{\bar 0}-v\gamma\vec e_{\bar 1},\quad \vec e_1=-v\gamma\vec e_{\bar 0}+\gamma\vec e_{\bar 1},\quad \vec e_2=\vec e_{\bar 2},\quad \vec e_3=\vec e_{\bar 3}
key_equations.meaning: Application of Eq. 2.13; these are the arrows drawn in Figure 2.1.

key_equations.name: Basis law with velocity shown
key_equations.meaning: Makes explicit that Lambda depends only on the relative velocity.
key_equations.symbols: v velocity of O-bar relative to O

key_equations.name: Reverse basis law
key_equations.meaning: Swapping the roles of the frames reverses the velocity; Lambda is always built from the upper-index frame's velocity relative to the lower-index frame.

key_equations.name: Substitution giving an identity in O's basis
key_equations.meaning: Only O's basis appears, so the combined coefficient must reproduce e_alpha.

key_equations.name: Coefficient of e_nu
key_equations.meaning: Must equal 1 when nu = alpha and 0 otherwise.

key_equations.name: Inverse of a boost
key_equations.meaning: The boost with reversed velocity is the matrix inverse of the original boost.

key_equations.name: Inverse component law
key_equations.meaning: Components in O are recovered from those in O-bar with the reversed boost.

key_equations.name: Four-momentum
key_equations.meaning: Rest mass times four-velocity.

key_equations.name: Four-momentum components
key_equations.meaning: Time component is the energy in O; spatial components are the momentum in O.

key_equations.name: Four-velocity from the rest frame
key_equations.meaning: The four-velocity's components in O are the first column of the transformation from the rest frame O-bar to O.
key_equations.symbols: O-bar rest frame of the particle

key_equations.name: Components for motion along x
key_equations.meaning: Evaluated form of Eq. 2.21; the matrix used carries velocity -v (O relative to O-bar), which makes the x entry positive.

key_equations.name: Low-speed energy
key_equations.meaning: Rest energy plus Newtonian kinetic energy.

key_equations.name: Total four-momentum
key_equations.meaning: The conserved quantity: the same before and after every interaction.

key_equations.name: Centre-of-momentum frame
key_equations.meaning: Defines the frame with zero total spatial momentum.

key_equations.name: Magnitude of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Signed squared norm modelled on the interval.

key_equations.name: Invariance of magnitude
key_equations.meaning: Guaranteed because components transform like coordinate differences, whose interval is invariant. (The export drops the bars on the right side; confirmed and restored from the page 62 render.)

key_equations.name: Scalar product
key_equations.meaning: Minkowski inner product; invariant under Lorentz transformations.

key_equations.name: Polarization identity
key_equations.latex: (\vec A+\vec B)\cdot(\vec A+\vec B)=\vec A^2+\vec B^2+2\vec A\cdot\vec B
key_equations.meaning: Key step in the invariance proof: every term but the cross term is known to be invariant.

key_equations.name: Orthonormality of a frame basis
key_equations.meaning: Basis vectors of any inertial frame form an orthonormal tetrad; eta will become the metric tensor.

key_equations.name: Normalization of four-velocity
key_equations.meaning: Four-velocity is a unit timelike vector.

key_equations.name: Interval as a magnitude
key_equations.meaning: The Chapter 1 interval is the magnitude of the infinitesimal displacement.

key_equations.name: Proper time
key_equations.meaning: Proper time along a timelike world line in scalar-product form.

key_equations.name: Unit tangent
key_equations.latex: \frac{d\vec x}{d\tau}\cdot\frac{d\vec x}{d\tau}=\frac{d\vec x\cdot d\vec x}{(d\tau)^2}=-1,\qquad \frac{d\vec x}{d\tau}\underset{\rm MCRF}{\to}(1,0,0,0)
key_equations.meaning: dx/dtau is a unit timelike tangent equal to e_0 of the MCRF.

key_equations.name: Four-velocity as a derivative
key_equations.meaning: Operational formula for four-velocity along any timelike world line.

key_equations.name: Derivative of the normalization
key_equations.meaning: Constant norm forces the derivative to be orthogonal to U (proved in components in Exercise 2.29).

key_equations.name: Four-acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Four-acceleration is orthogonal to four-velocity, hence purely spatial in the MCRF.

key_equations.name: Mass shell
key_equations.meaning: Four-momentum magnitude fixes the rest mass.

key_equations.name: Energy-momentum relation
key_equations.meaning: Total energy in terms of rest mass and momentum (c = 1).

key_equations.name: Energy measured by an observer
key_equations.meaning: Invariant expression for the energy a given observer measures, computable in any frame.
key_equations.symbols: U_obs observer four-velocity; E-bar energy in the observer's frame

key_equations.name: Null photon path
key_equations.meaning: Photon world lines are null, so dtau = 0 and no four-velocity exists.

key_equations.name: Null photon momentum
key_equations.meaning: A photon moving along x with energy E has p^x = E.

key_equations.name: Planck relation
key_equations.meaning: Photon energy from frequency; the text prints h = 6.6256e-34 with units J s^-1, a misprint for J s.

key_equations.name: Boosted photon energy
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz-transform the time component of the photon four-momentum.

key_equations.name: Relativistic Doppler shift (collinear)
key_equations.meaning: Frequency measured by an observer receding along the photon's direction at speed v.

key_equations.name: Photon rest mass
key_equations.meaning: Null momentum is equivalent to zero rest mass.

key_equations.name: Speed of a massive particle from its momentum
key_equations.meaning: Velocity p/E of a massive particle stays below light speed at any finite energy.

key_equations.name: Composition of boosts (Exercise 2.13)
key_equations.meaning: Successive transformations multiply as matrices.

key_equations.name: Doppler shift at an angle (Exercise 2.25)
key_equations.meaning: General Doppler formula; theta measured from O's x axis; at theta = pi/2 gives the transverse shift.

key_equations.name: Compton formula (Exercise 2.32)
key_equations.meaning: Frequency of a photon scattered through angle theta by a charge initially at rest (c = 1).

figures.label: Figure 2.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: The basis vectors of both frames drawn in the spacetime diagram of the moving observer O-bar.
figures.visual_description: O-bar's axes are drawn rectangular: a vertical line labelled t-bar and a horizontal line labelled x-bar crossing at the origin, with short arrows e_0-bar pointing up the t-bar axis and e_1-bar pointing right along the x-bar axis. O's axes are two tilted straight lines through the same origin: the t axis leans up and to the left of vertical (and continues below the origin to the lower right), carrying an arrow e_0 pointing up-left; the x axis slopes down to the right below horizontal (continuing up-left above the origin), carrying an arrow e_1 pointing down-right. The two tilted axes are mirror images across the 45-degree line running from upper left to lower right, and the arrows e_0 and e_1 are visibly longer on the page than e_0-bar and e_1-bar.
figures.what_it_teaches: The algebraic basis law e_alpha = Lambda^beta-bar_alpha e_beta-bar does exactly what geometry demands: each frame's basis vectors lie along that frame's own axes. Because O moves in the negative x-bar direction relative to O-bar, O's axes tilt toward the upper-left/lower-right light line, and Euclidean arrow length on the page is not Minkowski length.
concepts: basis vectors of an inertial frame

redesign.idea: Two-frame basis explorer: both frames' axes and basis arrows on one diagram, with unit hyperbolae t^2 - x^2 = 1 and x^2 - t^2 = 1 drawn so every basis-vector tip visibly lands on them, plus a draggable test vector decomposed into parallelograms along each basis.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a velocity slider (-0.95 to 0.95) and toggles which observer is drawn with rectangular axes; they drag the tip of vector A anywhere. Live panels show A's components in both frames, the Lambda matrix with the entries used highlighted row-wise for components and column-wise for basis vectors, and the invariant A^2 that never changes.

figures.label: Figure 2.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: At event A on an accelerated world line, the four-velocity coincides with the time basis vector of the momentarily comoving frame, shown together with that frame's spatial basis vector.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (vertical) and x (horizontal). A single curved world line starts below the x axis, rises nearly vertically, and bends steadily to the right as it climbs, showing a particle accelerating in +x. A dot marks event A on the upper part of the curve. Two arrows leave A: one tangent to the curve pointing up and to the right, labelled e_0-bar = U, and a second shallower arrow pointing to the right and slightly upward, labelled e_1-bar. The two arrows lean toward each other, symmetric about the 45-degree direction.
figures.what_it_teaches: An accelerated particle has a different inertial rest frame at each event; the MCRF basis at A has its time vector along the world line's tangent (the four-velocity) and its space vector along that frame's line of simultaneity, tilted correspondingly.

redesign.idea: MCRF slider along an accelerated world line: an event marker rides a chosen world line (hyperbolic, sinusoidal wobble, or learner-sketched), carrying a small orthonormal basis, a light cone and the MCRF's own straight world line and simultaneity line.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the marker or scrubs proper time; the MCRF basis rotates hyperbolically, the straight inertial world line of the current MCRF peels away from the curve, and readouts show v, gamma, U components and the check U.U = -1. A 'freeze MCRF' button leaves ghost frames behind to compare successive rest frames.

figures.label: Figure 2.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: With several collisions, the set of momentum arrows an observer adds up at one instant is observer-dependent, but their resultant is a single four-vector whose components in different frames are related by a Lorentz transformation. (In the export the caption is split off from the figure and appears as a normal paragraph after the label.)
figures.visual_description: Axes t (vertical) and x (horizontal) meet at the origin, with a second pair of lines from the origin: a steep one labelled t-bar and a shallow one labelled x-bar, the axes of a frame moving in +x. To the right, two collision events are marked. Event A lies just below the x axis: one particle world line comes up to it from a dot far below, and two arrows leave it, one up-left and one up-right. Event B lies just above the x axis but below the x-bar line: two world lines arrive from dots at lower left and lower right and cross there, continuing as arrows up-right and up-left. Both events are below the x-bar line, while A is below and B above the x line.
figures.what_it_teaches: On O's slice t = 0 the particles counted are those after A and before B; on O-bar's slice t-bar = 0 they are those after both. Because each collision conserves four-momentum locally, both tallies give the same total vector, so conservation does not depend on a choice of simultaneity.

redesign.idea: Who is counted when: two spacelike-separated collisions with the actual momentum arrows, a sweepable simultaneity slice, and a side panel adding the momenta of every world-line segment the slice currently cuts.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets the observer velocity (tilting the slice) and its time offset. Segments crossing the slice light up; the side panel shows those four-momenta added head-to-tail in a (p^x, E) plane. The individual arrows change as the slice tilts past A or B, but the resultant arrow stays fixed; a toggle breaks conservation at B to show the totals then disagree between observers.

figures.label: Figure 2.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: In O's diagram the basis vectors of a moving frame do not look perpendicular, but their Minkowski scalar product is zero.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (vertical, arrowed) and x (horizontal, arrowed) of frame O. From the origin two arrows point into the first quadrant: a steep one labelled e_0-bar rising up and to the right, and a shallower one labelled e_1-bar pointing to the right and upward. The angle between them is clearly acute, and they sit symmetrically on either side of the (undrawn) 45-degree line.
figures.what_it_teaches: Orthogonality in spacetime is not Euclidean perpendicularity: vectors are orthogonal when they make equal angles with a light ray's 45-degree line, so as the boost speed grows they close in on the light line and a null vector is orthogonal to itself.

redesign.idea: Minkowski protractor: the learner draws any vector and the app instantly draws its Minkowski-orthogonal partner as the reflection across the light line, alongside its Euclidean perpendicular for contrast.
redesign.interaction: Drag a vector's tip; readouts show both the Euclidean angle between the pair and their Minkowski dot product (always zero for the reflected partner). Dragging toward the light cone makes the vector and its partner converge onto the null line, where the vector becomes its own partner; a toggle switches the dot-product sign convention to show the Euclidean case.

figures.label: Figure 2.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: The infinitesimal displacement along a world line is a vector tangent to it.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (vertical, arrowed) and x (horizontal, arrowed). A curved world line crosses the x axis to the right of the origin, climbs steeply and bends gradually to the right. From a point partway up the curve a short straight arrow labelled dx leaves along the tangent, pointing up and slightly right, separating a little from the curve near its tip.
figures.what_it_teaches: The displacement between neighbouring events on a world line becomes tangent in the infinitesimal limit; dividing it by dtau gives a unit tangent, the four-velocity.

redesign.idea: Secant-to-tangent zoom: two events on a world line joined by a displacement arrow, with the arrow rescaled by the proper time between them.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the second event toward the first (or uses a shrink slider); the secant arrow Delta x turns into the tangent while Delta tau and the rescaled arrow Delta x / Delta tau are shown, the latter converging to a vector whose tip sits on the unit hyperbola centred at the base event.

worked_examples.label: An example (boost of components and basis)
worked_examples.problem: O-bar moves at speed v along x relative to O. Find the O-bar components of a vector with O components (5, 0, 0, 2), and express O's basis vectors in terms of O-bar's.
worked_examples.method: Write the x-boost matrix with gamma; apply the component law row by row; apply the basis law e_alpha = Lambda^beta-bar_alpha e_beta-bar, which reads down a column; sketch the result in O-bar's diagram.
worked_examples.key_insight: The same matrix is used in two different index patterns for components and for basis vectors, and the resulting basis vectors of O lie along O's tilted axes as seen by O-bar; y and z parts are untouched and the matrix is symmetric.
worked_examples.result: A -> (5 gamma, -5 v gamma, 0, 2) in O-bar; e_0 = gamma e_0-bar - v gamma e_1-bar, e_1 = -v gamma e_0-bar + gamma e_1-bar, e_2 = e_2-bar, e_3 = e_3-bar.

worked_examples.label: Derivation of the basis transformation law
worked_examples.problem: Given the component law, find how the basis vectors of O are related to those of O-bar.
worked_examples.method: Equate A^alpha e_alpha with A^alpha-bar e_alpha-bar; insert A^alpha-bar = Lambda^alpha-bar_beta A^beta; reorder the finite sums; rename beta to alpha and alpha-bar to beta-bar; factor out A^alpha; use arbitrariness of A to set the bracket to zero.
worked_examples.key_insight: Relabelling dummy indices is what lets the arbitrary components be isolated; arbitrariness of A turns one vector equation into a law for each basis vector.

worked_examples.label: Inverse transformation from reversed velocity
worked_examples.problem: Show that the Lorentz matrix with velocity -v is the inverse of that with v, and invert the component law.
worked_examples.method: Write e_alpha in terms of e_beta-bar with Lambda(v) and e_beta-bar in terms of e_nu with Lambda(-v); substitute to express e_alpha through O's own basis; demand the coefficient be 1 for nu = alpha and 0 otherwise; multiply the component law by Lambda(-v) and contract.
worked_examples.key_insight: An equation that mentions only one frame's basis must be an identity, which pins down a matrix product as the Kronecker delta; summing on a shared index is matrix multiplication.
worked_examples.result: Lambda^nu_beta-bar(-v) Lambda^beta-bar_alpha(v) = delta^nu_alpha and A^nu = Lambda^nu_beta-bar(-v) A^beta-bar.

worked_examples.label: An example (four-velocity and four-momentum of a moving particle)
worked_examples.problem: A particle of rest mass m moves at speed v along x of frame O. Find its four-velocity and four-momentum components, and interpret p^0 at low speed.
worked_examples.method: In the rest frame O-bar, U = e_0-bar and p = mU; transform to O so U^alpha is the first column of Lambda from O-bar to O; expand gamma for small v.
worked_examples.key_insight: Defining a physical vector by its trivial form in the rest frame lets the transformation law generate its components anywhere; the low-speed limit validates the names velocity, momentum and energy.
worked_examples.result: U = (gamma, v gamma, 0, 0), p = (m gamma, m v gamma, 0, 0); E = m gamma which is approximately m + m v^2/2.

worked_examples.label: Invariance of the scalar product
worked_examples.problem: Prove that A.B defined in one frame has the same value in every frame.
worked_examples.method: Note A.A and B.B are invariant magnitudes, as is (A+B).(A+B); expand the latter into A^2 + B^2 + 2A.B and conclude the cross term is invariant.
worked_examples.key_insight: Invariance of a bilinear form follows from invariance of its quadratic form, so no matrix algebra is needed.
concepts: Lorentz invariance of the scalar product

worked_examples.label: Examples: orthonormal bases and U.U = -1
worked_examples.problem: Evaluate the scalar products of a frame's basis vectors, check the result for a moving frame's basis drawn in O's diagram, and deduce the norm of any four-velocity.
worked_examples.method: Use component definitions in the frame's own coordinates to get eta; since the argument works in any frame, the moving basis is also orthonormal although the arrows look non-perpendicular (Figure 2.4); a four-velocity is a time basis vector.
worked_examples.key_insight: Orthonormality is frame independent, but its picture is not Euclidean: equal angles to the light line replace right angles.

worked_examples.label: Four-velocity and four-acceleration as derivatives
worked_examples.problem: Show that dx/dtau is the four-velocity and that the four-acceleration dU/dtau is orthogonal to it.
worked_examples.method: Compute the magnitude of dx/dtau using dtau^2 = -dx.dx; evaluate it in the MCRF where dtau = dt; then differentiate U.U = -1 with the product rule and read off components in the MCRF.
worked_examples.key_insight: A vector of constant magnitude has a derivative orthogonal to itself, and in the MCRF being orthogonal to U means having no time component. (The comparison with uniform circular motion in the plane is a tutoring analogy, not something the book draws.)
worked_examples.result: U = dx/dtau; a = dU/dtau with U.a = 0 and a = (0, a^1, a^2, a^3) in the MCRF.

worked_examples.label: Energy-momentum relation and observer energy
worked_examples.problem: Relate a particle's energy to its momentum and rest mass, and find the energy measured by an arbitrary observer.
worked_examples.method: Compute p.p = m^2 U.U = -m^2 and expand in components; for an observer, note U_obs is that observer's e_0-bar and evaluate p.e_0-bar in the observer's frame.
worked_examples.key_insight: A frame-specific quantity (energy relative to an observer) can be written as an invariant scalar product, which is then computable in whatever frame is convenient.

worked_examples.label: Photon momentum and the Doppler shift
worked_examples.problem: A photon of frequency nu travels along x in O. Find its frequency in O-bar moving at v along x.
worked_examples.method: Build p = (E, E, 0, 0) with E = h nu; apply the boost to the time component; set the result equal to h nu-bar.
worked_examples.key_insight: Once light has a four-momentum, the Doppler effect is just a Lorentz transformation plus E = h nu.
worked_examples.result: nu-bar/nu = (1-v)/sqrt(1-v^2) = sqrt((1-v)/(1+v)); for example v = 0.6 halves the frequency (dossier's own illustration).

worked_examples.label: Why massive particles stay below light speed
worked_examples.problem: Show that no amount of energy brings a massive particle to v = 1, while a massless one always moves at v = 1.
worked_examples.method: From p.p = -m^2 for motion along x, write p^1/p^0 = sqrt(1 - m^2/(p^0)^2); compare with p^1/p^0 = 1 for a null momentum; identify the frame moving at p^1/p^0 as a rest frame.
worked_examples.key_insight: The ratio p/E is the velocity; the mass term keeps it strictly below 1 for any finite E, and a rest frame exists exactly when m is not zero.
worked_examples.result: v = p/E < 1 for m > 0; v = 1 and no rest frame for m = 0.
concepts: light speed as an unreachable limit for massive particles

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A Euclidean arrow keeps its identity when the coordinate axes are rotated; only its components change.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The chapter opens by importing this Euclidean picture and then enforces it with notation: the vector symbol never gets a bar, only its indices do. Footnote 1 names it a passive transformation.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In spacetime the 'rotation' is a boost that tilts axes toward the light line and stretches arrows on the page, so Euclidean length and angle intuition fails even though the object-versus-components idea survives.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split screen: a 2D Euclidean rotation and a Minkowski boost applied to the same arrow, with component readouts changing and the arrow fixed in both panels.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Galilean velocity is a tangent to a particle's spatial path; four-velocity is a tangent to its world line in spacetime.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates the definition of U and its length condition (one unit of the particle's own time).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Galilean velocity can have any length; four-velocity is fixed at unit timelike norm and so cannot encode speed through its length, only through its tilt.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph a 3D path with velocity arrows into a world line with four-velocity arrows whose tips all lie on the unit hyperbola.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The magnitude of a vector is built exactly like the interval between two events.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives invariance for free, since components transform like coordinate differences.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The resulting 'length' can be negative or zero for nonzero vectors, unlike any Euclidean length.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: eta is a Kronecker delta with a minus sign in the time slot.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Lets the reader handle eta by familiar rules before it is recognized as a tensor.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Unlike delta, eta has two lower indices and changes form in non-inertial or non-orthonormal bases; the analogy hides its geometric role as the metric.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Summing over a shared index between two Lambdas is ordinary row-times-column matrix multiplication.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Translates Eq. 2.18 into the familiar statement that one matrix is the inverse of another.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Index notation is more general: it tracks which index is summed and handles objects with more than two indices where matrix pictures break down.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Hover over an index expression to highlight the corresponding row and column in two matrices and the resulting entry.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Orthogonal vectors on a spacetime diagram are mirror images across the 45-degree light line.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offers a drawing rule that replaces right angles for the t-x plane, explaining Figure 2.4 and the self-orthogonality of null vectors.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Valid as stated only for vectors lying in one t-x plane of the diagram; in more dimensions or with other orientations it must be generalized.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Mirror tool: reflecting any drawn vector across the light line produces its orthogonal partner, with a live dot-product meter.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Each observer takes a snapshot slice of spacetime and adds up the momenta of whatever particles cross it.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames the question of when to total momenta and shows the answer is slice independent if every collision conserves momentum.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The snapshot picture only works when all interactions are local events; with extended fields or curved spacetime the bookkeeping needs fluxes through boundaries (developed in Chapter 4).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The CM frame is to a system of particles what the MCRF is to a single particle.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The definition explicitly echoes the MCRF remark that any frame at rest relative to it also qualifies.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A CM frame exists only for a timelike total momentum; a lone photon, or photons all moving the same way, has none.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Transforming to another frame produces a different vector, so it should get a new symbol.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The vector is the same geometric object; only its components change, which is why the bar goes on the index.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Components are what we compute with, and they do change.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A dummy Greek index can be renamed to any letter, including a Latin one.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Latin indices run only over 1-3, so replacing a Greek dummy by a Latin one drops the time term.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The rule 'dummy names are arbitrary' sounds unconditional.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A free index can be renamed on one side of an equation only.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A free index must be renamed consistently in every term, otherwise the equation no longer links matching components.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Renaming dummies is local to a term, and learners overgeneralize.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A^alpha e_alpha and A^alpha-bar e_alpha-bar differ only by relabelling dummy indices.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Barred and unbarred indices refer to different frames; the component sets and the basis sets both differ, and only the sums agree.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both look like a sum over a repeated index.
concepts: basis vectors of an inertial frame

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Basis vectors transform with the same law as components.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The basis law e_alpha = Lambda^beta-bar_alpha e_beta-bar uses the matrix the other way round, precisely so that component and basis changes cancel in A^alpha e_alpha.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both involve the same Lambda and look superficially alike.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The inverse transformation needs a fresh matrix inversion, or the sign of v in a given Lambda is arbitrary.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The inverse is the same boost with -v, and each Lambda's velocity is the motion of its upper-index frame as judged from its lower-index frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Two frames and two directions of transformation make sign bookkeeping confusing.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any quadruple of physical quantities, such as (1, v_x, v_y, v_z) or (t, E, p, m), is automatically a four-vector.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Four numbers in one frame define a four-vector only when their values in every other frame are, by definition, given by the Lorentz rule; physically measured quantities must be checked to transform that way, and all components must share dimensions.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text remarks that any four same-dimensioned numbers make a vector, which is true as a definition but not a license to assemble arbitrary physical quantities.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A particle has a unique momentarily comoving frame.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: At a given event there are infinitely many MCRFs, all with the same velocity, differing by spatial rotations; the ambiguity rarely matters.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Rest mass is separately conserved in collisions, as in Newtonian mechanics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only total four-momentum is conserved; rest mass counts as energy and can be turned into kinetic energy and heat, as in nuclear reactors.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian physics treats mass conservation and energy conservation as independent laws.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since observers disagree on which collisions have happened 'by now', they must disagree about the total momentum.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Each collision conserves four-momentum locally, so the total over any observer's constant-time slice is the same vector; only its components differ.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Relativity of simultaneity really does change which particles are counted.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A vector with zero magnitude must be the zero vector, and magnitudes are never negative.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Minkowski magnitude is indefinite: timelike vectors have negative magnitude, and null vectors have zero magnitude with nonzero components.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Every inner product met before (Euclidean) is positive definite.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Orthogonal vectors must appear at right angles on a spacetime diagram.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Minkowski orthogonality shows up as symmetry about the light line; a moving frame's basis vectors look acutely angled yet are orthogonal, and a null vector is orthogonal to itself.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Paper diagrams are Euclidean, so our eyes measure Euclidean angles.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Photons have a four-velocity like other particles, just with speed 1.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Null world lines have dtau = 0 and no unit tangent, and light has no rest frame, so four-velocity is undefined; tangent vectors like dx or p still exist.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Photons obviously move and have a direction.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Four-momentum, like four-velocity, is a unit vector.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: p = mU has magnitude -m^2, and for photons it is null; its components carry energy and momentum, not a normalization.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: p is defined as a multiple of the unit vector U.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: With enough energy a massive particle can reach the speed of light.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its velocity p/E = sqrt(1 - m^2/E^2) stays below 1 for every finite energy, and it always keeps a rest frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Accelerator particles get arbitrarily close to c, and classical intuition says more push means more speed without bound.
concepts: light speed as an unreachable limit for massive particles
