misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Neutrinos (and gravitons) are established massless particles alongside the photon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Neutrinos have small but nonzero masses; the graviton is not a well-defined notion without a quantum theory of gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Older textbooks listed neutrinos as massless, and gravitational waves do travel at light speed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The four-acceleration has zero time component in every frame.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only in the MCRF is it purely spatial; in general frames U.a = 0 couples its time and space components.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter shows its components only in the MCRF.

thought_experiments.name: Two collisions seen from two slices
thought_experiments.setup: Two unrelated collisions A and B occur at spacelike-separated events. Observer O's t = 0 slice passes after A but before B; a moving observer O-bar's slice passes after both; some third frame reverses their order.
thought_experiments.lesson: The sets of particles counted differ between observers, but because momentum is conserved at each collision, every observer's total is the same four-vector.
thought_experiments.app_idea: See the Figure 2.3 redesign: a tilting slice with a live momentum-sum panel.

thought_experiments.name: Chasing a photon
thought_experiments.setup: Try to find an inertial frame in which a photon is at rest, or to normalize its world-line tangent to unit length.
thought_experiments.lesson: Neither is possible: the second postulate forbids the frame and a null tangent cannot be normalized, so photons have no four-velocity.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Boost slider applied to a photon's world line: the line stays at 45 degrees for every boost while a massive particle's world line can be made vertical.

thought_experiments.name: Pumping energy into a massive particle
thought_experiments.setup: Keep adding energy to a particle of rest mass m moving along x and track p^1/p^0.
thought_experiments.lesson: The ratio creeps toward but never reaches 1; the particle always has a rest frame, unlike a photon.
concepts: light speed as an unreachable limit for massive particles
thought_experiments.app_idea: Energy dial with a plot of v = p/E versus E/m approaching the asymptote 1, and the particle's mass hyperbola in the (p, E) plane.

thought_experiments.name: Hot body versus cold body
thought_experiments.setup: Exercise 2.27: two identical 10 kg bodies, one given 100 J of heat, are pushed by equal forces.
thought_experiments.lesson: Added internal energy adds inertia, so the heated body accelerates very slightly less.

thought_experiments.name: One-g rocket to the Galactic centre
thought_experiments.setup: Exercise 2.19: a rocket keeps a constant proper acceleration of about 10 m/s^2 from rest and travels about 2e20 m.
thought_experiments.lesson: Coordinate speed saturates below light speed while proper time grows only logarithmically with distance, so the crew ages far less than the travel time seen from Earth.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Dual clocks and a hyperbolic world line: Earth time, ship time and distance advance together with a slider for proper acceleration.

historical_notes.event: The implied-sum rule for repeated upper and lower indices is named after Einstein.
historical_notes.significance: The convention adopted here is used on nearly every later page of the book.

historical_notes.event: Photon energy proportional to frequency, E = h nu, is imported from quantum theory to connect four-momentum with frequency.
historical_notes.significance: Lets the Doppler shift follow from a single Lorentz transformation.

historical_notes.event: Exercise 2.32 names the scattering of photons by charged particles after Compton and asks for its frequency formula from four-momentum conservation.
historical_notes.significance: A classic experimental confirmation that photons carry relativistic four-momentum.

historical_notes.event: The text states that neutrinos are very light but not massless and that the graviton is not yet a well-defined concept.
historical_notes.significance: Reflects the modern (post neutrino-oscillation) particle picture, correcting the older habit of listing neutrinos among massless particles.

applications_and_observations.topic: Nuclear power as conversion of rest mass
applications_and_observations.details: Cited as everyday evidence that energy conservation must include rest mass, which can be reduced with the difference released as heat.

applications_and_observations.topic: Particle physics as the sharpest test of special relativity
applications_and_observations.details: The bibliography notes that relativistic kinematics underlies particle physics, which provides the most stringent tests of the theory.
The photon is the only known particle with zero rest mass; neutrinos are very light but have mass.
Value quoted with E = h nu for the Doppler discussion; the printed unit J s^-1 should read J s.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: h = 6.6256e-34 J s (modern value 6.62607015e-34 J s)

applications_and_observations.details: Plugging numbers into Eq. 2.39 shows how quickly the shift grows with receding speed.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: v = 0.6 gives nu-bar/nu = 0.5; v = 0.8 gives 1/3.

applications_and_observations.topic: Relativistic rocket at one Earth gravity (Exercise 2.19)
applications_and_observations.details: Constant proper acceleration 10 m/s^2 from rest; speed after coordinate time t, time to reach v = 0.999, and proper time for a trip to the Galactic centre.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate (accelerating the whole way): c/g is about 0.95 yr; reaching v = 0.999 takes about 21 yr of Earth time but about 3.6 yr of ship time; covering 2e20 m takes about 10 yr of ship time.

applications_and_observations.topic: Inverse-Compton upscattering of the microwave background (Exercise 2.33)
applications_and_observations.details: A 2e-4 eV background photon scatters off a cosmic-ray proton of 1e18 eV (gamma about 1e9) in the solar frame; the exercise asks for the maximum outgoing photon energy using the Compton formula in the proton frame.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: head-on back-scatter gives roughly 4 gamma^2 times 2e-4 eV, about 8e14 eV, i.e. a very-high-energy gamma ray; proton recoil in its rest frame is negligible (photon energy there about 0.4 MeV versus 938 MeV).

applications_and_observations.details: 100 J of heat added to a 10 kg body.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: mass increase 100 J / c^2 = 1.1e-15 kg, a fractional change of about 1.1e-16 in acceleration under equal force.

applications_and_observations.topic: Cosmic-ray energy measured aboard a rocket (Exercise 2.30)
applications_and_observations.details: Rocket four-velocity (2,1,1,1) and cosmic-ray four-momentum (300, 299, 0, 0) x 1e-27 kg; energy seen by passengers via -P.U.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: -P.U = (300 x 2 - 299 x 1) x 1e-27 kg = 3.01e-25 kg, about 2.7e-8 J (roughly 170 GeV).

applications_and_observations.topic: Where the Newtonian energy approximation fails (Exercise 2.23)
applications_and_observations.details: Next term in the expansion of E is 3mv^4/8; the exercise asks when it reaches half the kinetic term.

notation_and_conventions.convention: An arrow over a symbol marks a four-vector (x-arrow has nothing to do with the coordinate x); boldface marks a three-vector; 'vector' means four-vector unless stated.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Boldface convention is in footnote 2, dropped by the export.

notation_and_conventions.convention: A ->_O (A^0, A^1, A^2, A^3) means 'A has these components in frame O'; it is not an equality between a vector and numbers.
Components listed as (t, x, y, z), i.e. indices 0, 1, 2, 3.
A bar on an index (A^alpha-bar, e_alpha-bar) refers to frame O-bar; the vector symbol itself is never barred. A double bar denotes a third frame in the exercises.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The export often renders the bar as a tilde; the printed book uses bars.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Repeated index, once up and once down, is summed; basis vectors carry lower indices so A^alpha e_alpha sums.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Index positions are justified only in later chapters.

notation_and_conventions.item: Lambda index placement and velocity argument
notation_and_conventions.convention: Lambda^alpha-bar_beta takes O components to O-bar components; the argument v of Lambda(v) is the motion of the frame on the upper index as measured from the frame on the lower index.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In Eq. 2.21 Lambda^alpha_0-bar therefore carries the velocity of O relative to the rest frame.

notation_and_conventions.convention: c = 1 inherited from Chapter 1; speeds are dimensionless, and energy, momentum and mass share units (the exercises quote four-momenta in kg).
notation_and_conventions.notes: G is not needed in this chapter.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Scalar product and eta use signature (-, +, +, +): eta_00 = -1, eta_ii = +1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Consequently timelike vectors have negative magnitude and unit timelike vectors have magnitude -1.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The word 'magnitude' and the symbol A^2 denote the signed quantity A.A itself, not a square root.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Differs from the Euclidean habit of calling |A| the magnitude.

notation_and_conventions.convention: p^0 = E, spatial momentum p^i; for photons p^x, p^y, p^z are used; E-bar denotes energy in the observer's frame.
Parenthesized subscripts such as p_(i) label particles and are not tensor indices, so no summation is implied by them.
MCRF = momentarily comoving reference frame; CM = centre of momentum; U_obs = four-velocity of an observer.

margin_notes.summary: Footnote 1 (lost in the export, read from the render): changing frames in this way is the linear-algebra notion of a passive transformation, where only the coordinate description changes and the arrow stays fixed.

Footnote 2 (lost in the export, read from the render): introduces the name four-vector, contrasts it with the three-vectors of elementary physics, says 'vector' will mean four-vector by default, and fixes the typography: arrows for four-vectors, boldface for three-vectors.
Opening promise that a more satisfactory definition of vector will come later (realized as tangent vectors to curves on manifolds).
Reason for writing one Lambda index up and one down is deferred to differential geometry.
Reader is told to compare Figure 2.1 with Chapter 1's Figure 1.5(b), the same two frames drawn from the moving observer's viewpoint.
Exercise 2.11 is recommended for mastering which velocity sign goes into each Lambda.
Parenthetical caution that an accelerated particle has infinitely many MCRFs at an event, related by spatial rotations.
Warning that the reasoning about totals on constant-time hypersurfaces will recur with later conservation laws.
eta is announced as the metric tensor, to be treated properly later.
Exercise 2.19 is cited as the justification for calling dU/dtau an acceleration.
Aside that the graviton is sometimes listed as massless but is not yet well defined without quantum gravity; neutrinos are light but massive.
Bibliography: Hagedorn (1963) and Wiedemann (2007) for relativistic kinematics and particle dynamics.

identifying and renaming free and dummy indices
transforming components between frames and checking invariance of magnitudes and dot products

drawing basis vectors of moving frames on spacetime diagrams
computing four-velocity and four-acceleration for given world lines

notable.summary: Compose a boost of 0.6 along x with a boost of 0.8 along the intermediate frame's y axis, verify the product preserves the interval, then explain why the result is not symmetric and why reversing the order gives a different matrix.
notable.why_notable: The only place the chapter hints that two non-collinear boosts include a rotation (Thomas-Wigner), which matters for spin precession and gyroscopes later.

notable.summary: Define uniform acceleration via the four-acceleration, show it matches a constant felt acceleration, and follow a 10 m/s^2 rocket: speed and distance versus time, time to reach 0.999, proper time elapsed, and ageing on a trip to the Galactic centre.
notable.why_notable: Turns abstract four-acceleration into the classic relativistic rocket, with dramatic numbers and a direct link to Rindler observers used later.

notable.summary: Analyse the world line t = a sinh(lambda/a), x = a cosh(lambda/a): show lambda is proper time, the four-acceleration is uniform, and interpret the constant a.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the uniformly accelerated world line that Exercise 5.21 builds on when constructing an accelerated observer's coordinates.

notable.summary: Use four-momentum conservation to prove an electron-positron pair cannot annihilate into one photon, while two photons are allowed.
notable.why_notable: A crisp demonstration that invariant magnitudes forbid reactions without any detailed dynamics.

notable.summary: Derive the Doppler formula for a photon travelling at an angle, identify the transverse Doppler shift, find the angle of zero shift, and rederive it with -p.U_obs.
notable.why_notable: Generalizes Eq. 2.39 and exposes time dilation hidden in the Doppler effect.

notable.summary: Compute the energy of a cosmic ray measured by rocket passengers both by constructing the boost to the rocket's frame and via -P.U, then compare the effort.
notable.why_notable: Makes the reader feel the payoff of the chapter's advice to use invariant expressions.

notable.summary: Apply the Compton formula in the rest frame of a 1e18 eV cosmic-ray proton to a microwave-background photon and find the maximum photon energy back in the solar frame, naming its band.
notable.why_notable: Links chapter kinematics to inverse-Compton production of high-energy gamma rays in astrophysics.

notable.summary: Check that the basis vectors produced by the reversed-velocity transformation of Eq. 2.15 still satisfy e-bar_alpha . e-bar_beta = eta_alpha-beta.
notable.why_notable: Confirms that boosts carry orthonormal tetrads to orthonormal tetrads, the property that defines Lorentz transformations.

difficulty.notes: Mathematically light (linear combinations, matrix products, a product-rule derivative), but the index gymnastics are new to most readers and the frame-labelling of Lambda matrices is a genuine source of sign errors. Conceptually the hardest ideas are object-versus-components, indefinite orthogonality, and conservation independent of simultaneity. Explanations are slow and explicit, with many small examples; the text is terse only on the provisional nature of the vector definition and on four-acceleration in general frames. Export issues: footnotes 1-2 are missing from the reading copy, the Figure 2.3 caption is detached from its figure and appears as an ordinary paragraph, and bars are often transcribed as tildes or dropped (e.g. the right side of Eq. 2.25).

cross_references.reason: Invariant interval (Eq. 1.1) is the model for the magnitude of a vector and reappears as ds^2 = dx.dx.
Proper time definition (Eq. 1.9) rewritten as dtau^2 = -dx.dx.
Lorentz transformation (Eq. 1.12) supplies the Lambda coefficients; Exercise 2.11 starts from it.
Figure 1.5(b), the two frames drawn from O-bar's viewpoint, is the axis picture behind Figure 2.1.
Second postulate used to show light has no rest frame and hence no four-velocity.
Velocity-addition law rederived with four-velocities in Exercise 2.16.
eta_alpha-beta is promoted to the metric tensor g, a machine taking two vectors to their scalar product.
One-forms and lower indices explain why Lambda and basis vectors carry the index positions introduced here.
The observer-energy formula Eq. 2.35 is recast with one-forms so the awkward minus sign disappears, and Exercise 4.4 reuses the same pattern (-N.U_obs) for number density.
Conservation laws over constant-time hypersurfaces return as Gauss' law for particle number and energy-momentum.
Each fluid element is assigned an MCRF in the sense of §2.3, and scalars such as number density are defined in it; four-velocity then builds the number-flux vector of §4.2.
The photon Doppler formula underlies the gravitational-redshift argument, and the hyperbolic world line of Exercise 2.21 is the starting point of Exercise 5.21 on accelerated observers.
The promised better definition of a vector: tangent vectors to curves on a manifold, with components dx^alpha/dlambda.
Four-momentum and the mass-shell condition p.p = -m^2 are carried into curved spacetime, where the chapter asks which momentum components stay conserved along geodesics.
Gravitational waves travel at light speed, prompting the chapter's aside about gravitons.
Recommended for relativistic kinematics and particle dynamics beyond this chapter.
Recommended for relativistic particle dynamics in accelerators.

teaching_gems.gem: Typographic separation of a vector from its components: the vector symbol never changes between frames, only the labelled 'has components' arrow and the bars on indices do.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners absorb the geometric-object idea through every line they write, not through a one-time definition, which prevents the common belief that a boost makes a new vector.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Notation-aware equation editor in the course: typing a barred vector symbol triggers a gentle tutor hint and the rendered arrow stays identical across frame tabs while component tables change.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive the basis transformation law from A^alpha e_alpha = A^alpha-bar e_alpha-bar by relabelling dummy indices and exploiting the arbitrariness of A.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows index notation as a reasoning engine, and explains why components and basis vectors must transform oppositely so that the vector stays put.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation widget where learners drag index letters to relabel dummies, with illegal moves (Latin replacement, unmatched free indices) flagged and explained.

teaching_gems.gem: Define four-velocity as the time basis vector of the rest frame or MCRF, then prove it equals dx/dtau.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives both a picture (a frame's time arrow riding along the world line) and a formula, and immediately explains U.U = -1 without computation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Figure 2.2 redesign: drag along a world line with the MCRF basis attached and a dx/dtau arrow overlaid to show they coincide.

teaching_gems.gem: Invariance of the dot product from invariance of magnitudes via (A+B)^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2A.B.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A three-line proof that transfers to any bilinear form and avoids opaque matrix algebra.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three draggable vectors A, B, A+B in two frames with live magnitudes; the cross term is computed from them and shown to agree across frames.

teaching_gems.gem: Orthogonal means mirror-symmetric about the light line; a null vector is orthogonal to itself.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces the misleading right-angle intuition with a drawable rule that also explains why boosted axes close like scissors toward the light cone.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Figure 2.4 redesign: Minkowski protractor with Euclidean comparison and self-orthogonality at the light cone.

teaching_gems.gem: Differentiate U.U = -1 to show four-acceleration is orthogonal to four-velocity.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Echoes the Euclidean fact that constant-speed circular motion has acceleration perpendicular to velocity, and lands a structural result in two lines.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Side-by-side: circular motion in the plane with v perpendicular to a, and hyperbolic motion in spacetime with U and a mirror-symmetric about the light line.

teaching_gems.gem: Energy measured by an observer is -p.U_obs, computable in any frame.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Teaches the habit of writing observables as scalars built from the observer's four-velocity, a technique that carries straight into curved spacetime where there is no global frame to boost into.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Observer picker: several observers with different four-velocities watch one particle; each observer's energy is shown both by boosting components and by the dot product, with matching numbers.

teaching_gems.gem: Resolve the 'before or after the collision' simultaneity puzzle by local conservation at each event.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Confronts a real worry that careful students raise and establishes conservation as a statement about spacetime rather than about a preferred time.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Figure 2.3 redesign with a tilting simultaneity slice and a running momentum sum.

teaching_gems.gem: Doppler shift in two lines from boosting a null four-momentum and applying E = h nu.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Demonstrates the efficiency of four-vector thinking compared with wave-crest or clock-signal derivations.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Photon four-momentum arrow in a (p^x, E) plane under a boost slider, with a colour bar showing the frequency change and the ratio sqrt((1-v)/(1+v)).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Planck's constant is printed with units J s^-1 instead of J s.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Dimensional-analysis checks on E = h nu fail or mislead.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the correct unit J s and the exact SI value 6.62607015e-34 J s.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 2.1 lists C_33 twice with conflicting values (-3 and 0).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot know which value to use and may think they misunderstand the notation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Flag the duplication and choose one value (or note both answers) in any adapted version of the exercise.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The reading-copy export drops footnotes 1-2, detaches the Figure 2.3 caption so it reads like body text, and transcribes many bars as tildes or drops them entirely (e.g. the barred right side of Eq. 2.25).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anything built only from the export will miss the passive-transformation remark and the four-vector/three-vector/boldface terminology, may treat the Figure 2.3 caption as a separate argument, and may misread frame labels.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use this dossier's recovered content; treat tildes in the export as bars.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The sign convention for Lambda is easy to get wrong: in Eq. 2.21 the matrix from the rest frame to O carries velocity -v, which is why U^1 = +v gamma, but this is left implicit.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students often obtain U^1 = -v gamma and conclude the book is wrong or that they misunderstand four-velocity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Always check a boost by transforming the rest-frame e_0: the result must point in the direction of motion. Make the 'upper-index frame relative to lower-index frame' rule an explicit checklist item.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Calling any four same-dimensioned numbers a vector is correct as a definition but invites treating arbitrary physical quadruples as four-vectors.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may build 'four-vectors' such as (1, v) or (E, x) that do not transform by Lorentz matrices.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair the definition with counterexamples and the test 'does this quantity in every frame equal Lambda applied to its values in one frame?'.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Conservation of four-momentum is simply postulated; no argument from collisions, symmetry or the principle of relativity is offered.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Its status can feel arbitrary, and learners do not see why mass-energy equivalence is forced rather than chosen.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Supplement with a symmetric elastic-collision argument viewed from two frames, or a brief pointer to translation symmetry, while keeping Schutz's point that experiment is the final arbiter.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The equal-angles-to-the-light-line orthogonality rule is stated without its restriction to vectors in a single t-x plane or a proof.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may misapply it to vectors with y or z components or doubt it without seeing why it works.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the two-line proof for (a, b) and (b, a) in the t-x plane and note the generalization needs the full dot product.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Using 'magnitude' and A^2 for the signed quantity A.A clashes with the usual meaning of magnitude as a non-negative length.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion when later texts or the same book speak of |A| or take square roots of magnitudes of timelike vectors.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'squared norm' or 'norm-squared' in the app and reserve |A| = sqrt(|A.A|) for lengths and durations.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The clock hypothesis (an accelerated clock ticks at the rate of its MCRF) is used implicitly when defining four-velocity and proper time for accelerated world lines.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may not realize this is a physical assumption supported by experiment (e.g. muon storage rings) rather than a mathematical identity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Name the assumption when introducing MCRFs and cite the experimental support.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Four-acceleration is analysed only in the MCRF; its components in a general frame and its relation to three-acceleration are left to Exercise 2.19.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may believe a^0 always vanishes or struggle to compute a from a given x(t).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a worked example for straight-line motion in the lab frame showing a = gamma^4 (dv/dt)(v, 1, 0, 0) and checking U.a = 0.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Doppler derivation does fix the geometry (photon along +x, O-bar moving at +v along x), but the text never says whether the result is a redshift or a blueshift or what changes for an approaching observer.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blue and red shift get swapped in applications.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say explicitly that O-bar is moving the same way as the photon, so for v > 0 it measures a lower frequency (redshift), and get the approaching case by replacing v with -v.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you rotate your graph paper, does the arrow you drew change?' Then ask what should replace rotation in spacetime. This sets up the object-versus-components distinction before any indices appear.

Teach notation in this order: frame-labelled component arrow, bars on indices, Lambda as a table of 16 numbers, summation convention, dummy versus free indices. Check each with a one-line relabelling quiz before moving on.
Before deriving Eq. 2.13, have the learner predict whether basis vectors should transform with Lambda or with its inverse, using the requirement that A itself must not change.

When learners get sign errors with boosts, have them transform e_0 of the moving frame into the lab frame: the spatial component must have the sign of the motion. Reinforce the rule: read the velocity in a Lambda as 'how the upper-index observer moves, seen by the lower-index observer'.
Present four-velocity first as the moving frame's time arrow (e_0 of the MCRF), then as dx/dtau, then compute gamma(1, v). Ask: 'Why is every four-velocity the same length?'
Check understanding of Minkowski orthogonality with a drawing task: sketch a vector at 30 degrees from the t axis and draw its orthogonal partner. Then ask what happens at 45 degrees.
Common question: 'If observers disagree about simultaneity, how can total momentum be conserved?' Walk through Figure 2.3: local conservation at each collision makes the slice irrelevant.

Common question: 'Does a photon experience zero time / have a rest frame?' Answer with dtau = 0, the absence of a unit tangent and the second postulate, and caution against talk of a photon's point of view.
Encourage the invariant route for observer quantities: whenever a problem says 'as measured by', look for a dot product with that observer's four-velocity. Exercise 2.30 is a good confidence builder.

For advanced learners, preview that eta becomes the metric tensor (ch3), that the minus-dot-product-with-U_obs pattern returns for fluid number density (ch4), and that four-momentum and p.p = -m^2 carry over to curved spacetime (ch7); for beginners, keep to t-x diagrams and numeric boosts with v = 0.6 (gamma = 1.25).

Quick checks: Is (3, 3, 0, 0) timelike, spacelike or null? Can two timelike vectors be orthogonal? What is -p.U for a particle at rest in the observer's frame? Why can't an electron-positron pair annihilate into a single photon?
